motion: America doesn't need a strong dollar policy

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Welcome to the debate on whether America does not need a strong dollar policy. Cecilia argues for the motion, and Claudia argues against it. Each gets thirty seconds to open, followed by two and a half minutes of crossfire, then thirty-second closings. I will give a ten-second cue, and I will enforce the time limits.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: A strong dollar policy sounds disciplined, but it makes our goods costlier abroad and rewards financial bets over productive work. It can also pull investment toward a currency goal rather than factories, training, and new ideas. I am arguing that America needs a flexible economy, not an official promise to keep the dollar high.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Well, now it's ten.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: The choice is not between strength and weakness. It is between a dollar guided by broad needs and one protected even when workers and exporters pay.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: I'm going to let her respond to that.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: A strong dollar protects purchasing power, lowers the cost of essential imports, and gives businesses confidence when they plan. Abandoning that policy invites instability and makes every paycheck less reliable. America needs a clear anchor, not a currency left to drift.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: As the conversation continues, we're going to give you each a chance to rebut one another. You get two and a half minutes from the moment I finish speaking. I will give you a ten-second warning.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Picture a family facing sharply higher prices for imported essentials after the dollar slides. Their budget shrinks before wages adjust, proving that a strong dollar policy protects ordinary households.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: That example assumes a policy can prevent every price increase, which it cannot. A small exporter losing a sale is concrete evidence that defending the dollar can punish American production.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: When inflation threatens household budgets, a strong dollar policy protects purchasing power better than deliberate weakness. Under that condition, keeping the currency firm is responsible policy.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Businesses also need predictable rules, and families need affordable goods. But predictability can come from sound institutions rather than a favored exchange rate; the motion is about rejecting that narrow policy.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: A reliable currency supports households and businesses across the economy, not just people buying imports. That broad benefit makes a strong dollar policy worth maintaining.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Your broad benefit does not answer the policy's cost. A reliable currency is valuable, but forcing it upward can weaken exporters, shift jobs away, and make that reliability too expensive.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Consider a school buying imported equipment: a stronger dollar lowers the bill, leaving more money for teachers and repairs. That practical gain proves currency strength can serve the public, not merely investors-

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: No, that unfinished example cannot hide the tradeoff. Cheaper equipment helps one buyer, while an official high-dollar goal burdens producers broadly; America does not need that policy.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: If officials stop supporting a strong dollar, what prevents a falling currency from raising import costs and eroding the purchasing power you say matters?

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: The premise is false: rejecting a strong dollar policy does not require seeking a falling currency. We can protect purchasing power while allowing the exchange rate to adjust when production needs it.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: I agree that adjustment is not the same as deliberate weakness. But without a firm policy, markets can overshoot, and families cannot wait for correction; a strong dollar offers needed protection.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: That point treats a possible overshoot as proof of permanent guidance. Temporary market risk is not a reason to make exporters and workers absorb an official high-dollar policy.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: A manufacturer importing crucial parts pays less when the dollar is strong, keeping its product affordable and its doors open. That benefit proves currency strength supports American jobs.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Your manufacturer example ignores companies selling abroad, which face the opposite pressure. One cheaper input does not justify a policy that makes American products less competitive.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Ten seconds, both of you.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: If a flexible dollar is so helpful, who protects families when its adjustment makes-

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Time. Now we move on to round three. Round three will be closing statements by each debater in turn. Making her closing statement in support of the resolution america does not need to maintain a strong dollar policy, Cecilia.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: This debate turns on whether America should favor one exchange-rate outcome. It should not; workers, exporters, and consumers need flexibility, not an official target.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: That leaves families exposed. A firm currency-

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Claudia, please. Thank you.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Families deserve stable prices, but a strong dollar policy is not the only tool for stability. It can also damage production and jobs, so America should keep its options open.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Ten.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Flexibility serves more Americans than an expensive promise to keep the dollar strong.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Okay, Cecilia, thank you Claudia.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: The decision turns on which risk deserves priority: the visible cost of a firm dollar to exporters, or the hidden cost of currency weakness to every household. A strong dollar policy gives families purchasing power, helps businesses price imported parts, and signals discipline. Flexibility sounds attractive, but it can become uncertainty when people are already struggling. The motion rejects a useful safeguard.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: You have ten seconds.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: America should not discard protection merely because it creates tradeoffs. A steady currency supports planning, limits sudden price shocks, and keeps household budgets-

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: I'm gonna cut you off just for time.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Thank you both for your thoughtful arguments. This debate is now closed, with no winner declared.
